Industrial clusters, which are geographical concentrations of manufacturing companies and businesses operating within related industries, are designed to promote industrial growth through shared infrastructure, access to markets, technology transfer and economies of scale.
However, across Nigeria, many of these clusters are struggling to deliver their intended economic benefits because the infrastructure required to support large-scale industrial activities remains inadequate.
From Agbara Industrial Estate in Ogun State to Aba’s leather and garment clusters in Abia State, as well as the Apapa and Ikeja industrial corridors in Lagos, manufacturers continue to contend with infrastructure challenges that increase production costs, delay deliveries and weaken their competitiveness.
The Nigerian Investment Promotion Commission (NIPC) estimated that the country’s infrastructure deficit stands at about $100 billion, describing it as a major constraint on productivity across different sectors of the economy.
Electricity remains one of the biggest challenges confronting manufacturers operating within industrial clusters.
Many factories depend on diesel generators, gas-powered plants and other alternative energy sources to maintain production because of unreliable public electricity supply.
This increases production costs, particularly for small and medium-sized manufacturers that lack the financial capacity to invest in independent power infrastructure.
The federal government’s recent industrial policy initiative has placed renewed emphasis on strengthening domestic production and addressing structural constraints confronting manufacturers.
President Bola Tinubu launched the Nigeria Industrial Policy 2025 on February 17, 2026, with a focus on improving industrial capacity, reducing import dependence and promoting manufacturing-led economic growth.
Speaking, the national president of the Association of Small Business Owners of Nigeria (ASBON), Dr Femi Egbesola, said a functional industrial cluster should be more than an industrial location where businesses operate side by side.
He stated that it should provide reliable electricity, good roads, water, security, affordable financing, shared production equipment, modern technology, testing laboratories, packaging facilities and access to markets.
Egbesola said small manufacturers should be able to share expensive machinery and production facilities instead of each business having to acquire them individually. He added that there should also be training centres, business development support and links with larger manufacturers to create supply-chain opportunities.
“This would reduce production costs, improve product quality and make small businesses more competitive,” he said.
The chief executive officer of the Centre for the Promotion of Private Enterprise (CPPE), Dr Muda Yusuf, said the clusters had been fairly beneficial, especially to small-scale industrialists.
“The fact that those places, many of them are still occupied, speaks to the fact that they are providing some useful value to industrialists, especially the small-scale industrialists,” Yusuf said.
But he said more empirical data was needed to measure their full impact, adding that complaints from operators were consistent, as many clusters lacked the basic facilities that were supposed to support them.
“The facilities in terms of infrastructure that are supposed to support those zones are not there. For some of them, they don’t have support in terms of electricity. Some of them, their internal roads are not so good,” he said.
He listed logistics, warehousing and power supply as key facilities missing in many clusters.
Egbesola agreed, citing unreliable electricity, poor roads, high operating costs, inadequate financing and limited access to modern technology as major constraints.
“Businesses may enjoy proximity to suppliers and customers, but they do not necessarily benefit from shared infrastructure, affordable production facilities and organised market support,” he said.
For energy-intensive sectors such as textiles, the burden is even heavier. The director-general of the Nigerian Textile Employers Association, Mr Kwajaffa Hamma, said competing countries subsidised power for textile parks and kept prices stable.
“If you are not discounted, if you are not competitive with other countries, then you will not be able to sell when you export to their countries,” Hamma said.
He said little had been done in Nigeria’s textile parks since they were conceived in 2009, and capital budgets were often not released.
The CPPE chief executive cited Ethiopia as a country doing well with industrial clusters, saying its clusters provided facilities that were not present in other parts of the country, so manufacturers did not have to worry about logistics and warehousing.
“When they produce, they are able to produce more competitively. That is what makes the cluster framework to be much more productive,” Yusuf said.
Egbesola pointed to India as a particularly relevant model for Nigeria, explaining that “through its Micro and Small Enterprises Cluster Development Programme (MSE-CDP), the Indian government supports businesses within clusters with
shared facilities, modern equipment, technology, infrastructure and skills development.
“Importantly, businesses do not have to individually shoulder the cost of facilities that can be shared,” he said.
Yusuf called on federal and state governments to spend a lot more on facilities in clusters, describing it as one of the best ways to support small-scale industrialists and small businesses.
Egbesola said the focus should be on shared infrastructure, affordable finance, skills and market linkages, not just allocating land.
